prayer.text: Our Lady of Lourdes, pray for us.

cues.text: A Family in the Cachot
Marie-Bernarde Soubirous was born January 7, 1844, the eldest of nine children of a failed miller in Lourdes, France.
By 1857 the family's fortunes had collapsed so completely that they lived in a single windowless room known locally as le cachot , "the dungeon", a disused jail cell rented from a cousin out of pity.
Bernadette suffered from severe asthma her whole life, stood barely four foot seven, and at fourteen could neither read nor write.
We see in her poverty not an obstacle Heaven overlooked but the very condition the Gospel calls blessed: hers was a life with nothing left to lose and everything left to receive.
A Lady at Massabielle
On February 11, 1858 , Bernadette went with her sister and a friend to gather firewood near the grotto of Massabielle on the outskirts of town.
Hearing a sound like a gust of wind, she looked up and saw a young woman, no older than sixteen or seventeen, standing in a niche in the rock.
She was dressed in white with a blue sash and a golden rose at each foot, holding a rosary of pearls.
Bernadette alone could see her.
She fell to her knees and began to pray, and the "Lady", as she would simply call her, smiled and beckoned her to return.
Eighteen Apparitions
Over the following five months, Bernadette reported eighteen apparitions in all, most of them at the grotto, drawing crowds that grew from a handful of the curious to thousands of the devout.
The Lady asked her, in the local Occitan dialect, to pray for sinners , to do penance for the conversion of the world, and to have a chapel built on the site.
On February 25 , the Lady directed her to a dry patch of ground and told her to drink and wash there.
Scraping at the earth with her own hands, Bernadette uncovered a spring that had never before flowed from that rock, and which flows still.
I Am the Immaculate Conception
For months Bernadette pressed the Lady to say who she was, and each time received only a smile.
Finally, on March 25, 1858 , the feast of the Annunciation, the Lady clasped her hands, raised her eyes to heaven, and answered.
Bernadette had almost certainly never heard the phrase and could not have understood its theological weight.
She ran to tell the parish priest exactly what she had heard, repeating the words to herself over and over along the way so as not to forget them.
The dogma of the Immaculate Conception had been solemnly defined by Pope Pius IX only four years earlier, in 1854.
Ridicule and Investigation
Civil authorities, embarrassed by the crowds and suspicious of fraud, tried repeatedly to intimidate Bernadette and even briefly threatened her family with prison.
The local clergy, no less cautious, subjected her to relentless, often hostile questioning.
Through it all Bernadette never altered a single detail of her account and asked for nothing for herself.

Her parish priest, Fr. Dominique Peyramale , initially skeptical, became her steadfast protector, relaying her simple, unwavering testimony to a diocesan commission that spent nearly four years examining every claim before rendering judgment.
A Cloistered Life, A Quiet Death
In 1866, seeking anonymity from the fame she had never sought, Bernadette entered the convent of the Sisters of Charity at Nevers, far from Lourdes and its growing crowds.

She served humbly as an infirmary aide, suffered constantly from tuberculosis of the bone and chronic asthma, and died on April 16, 1879 , at just thirty-five, having asked only to be forgotten by history.
When her body was exhumed decades later for the process of canonization, witnesses found it remarkably incorrupt, a quiet seal on a life that had sought no attention in this world.
Legacy
On January 18, 1862 , Bishop Bertrand-Sévère Laurence of Tarbes formally declared the apparitions worthy of belief, and Bernadette Soubirous was canonized a saint by Pope Pius XI in 1933.

The spring she uncovered now flows through the taps of a sanctuary visited by some five million pilgrims a year, and the Church has recognized dozens of medically inexplicable cures among the countless graces reported there.
Lourdes still says to every believer what it said to a poor, unlettered shepherd girl in 1858: God's tenderness needs no credentials.
The world's poorest and most overlooked remain, in the eyes of Heaven, exactly the ones worth searching out.
